key_points.point: The document suggests that AI should be viewed as a tool for human progress, similar to electricity or the internet. By focusing on AI as a 'normal technology,' it implies that we should continue to build and deploy these tools to solve complex problems. This aligns with the accelerationist view that AI is a revolutionary force for abundance, provided we maintain control and focus on beneficial applications.
key_points.verbatim: We articulate a vision of artificial intelligence (AI) as normal technology. To view AI as normal is not to understate its impact—even transformative, general-purpose technologies such as electricity and the internet are “normal” in our conception.

key_points.point: The authors argue that drastic policy interventions are unnecessary and that we should treat AI as a tool we can control. They emphasize that the focus should be on practical, iterative deployment rather than speculative, human-like intelligence. This supports the accelerationist preference for deploying systems, monitoring them, and iterating to find solutions rather than pausing for theoretical debates.
key_points.verbatim: We view AI as a tool that we can and should remain in control of, and we argue that this goal does not require drastic policy interventions or technical breakthroughs.

key_points.point: The document suggests that the control problem is likely manageable if AI systems are not significantly more capable than human-AI teams. It argues that focusing on extreme scenarios like superintelligence distracts from more practical engineering approaches to control. Accelerationists would view this as a validation of their focus on building and iterating rather than pausing.
key_points.verbatim: But, if we are correct that AI systems will not be meaningfully more capable than humans acting with AI assistance, then the control problem is much more tractable, especially if superhuman persuasion turns out to be an unfounded concern.

key_points.point: The document argues that human-in-the-loop control is often an extreme and impractical model that hinders automation benefits. It suggests that auditing, monitoring, and system safety engineering are more effective ways to manage AI. This aligns with the accelerationist preference for practical, iterative safety over rigid, pre-deployment constraints.
key_points.verbatim: In most scenarios, this approach greatly diminishes the benefits of automation, and therefore either devolves into the human acting as a rubber stamp or is outcompeted by a less safe solution.

key_points.point: The document supports adapting existing engineering disciplines like system safety and cybersecurity for AI control. It advocates for techniques like fail-safes, circuit breakers, and least-privilege access. This supports the accelerationist view that AI safety is an engineering challenge that can be solved through standard technical practices.
key_points.verbatim: Other ideas come from system safety, an engineering discipline that is focused on preventing accidents in complex systems through systematic analysis and design.

key_points.point: The document argues that open-source AI models are a powerful tool for safety and innovation. By allowing thousands of independent researchers to probe for flaws, biases, and vulnerabilities, open-source development creates a feedback loop that accelerates progress. This approach prevents monopolistic control by a few large companies and democratizes access to transformative technology.
key_points.verbatim: Open-sourcing AI models is the single most effective way to improve safety, because it allows thousands of independent researchers to probe for flaws, biases, and vulnerabilities that any single company would miss.

This supports the accelerationist view that we have time to iterate and that current safety mechanisms are already functioning as speed limits.

key_points.verbatim: Marchant and Stevens described four approaches to governing emerging technologies; see Figure 7. Two are ex ante, risk analysis and precaution, and the other two are ex post, liability and resilience.

key_points.verbatim: Resilience combines elements of ex ante and ex post approaches, and consists of taking actions before harm occurs in order to be in a better position to limit the damage when harm does occur.

key_points.verbatim: In fact, there are (credible) concerns that existing regulation of high-risk AI is so onerous that it may lead to “runaway bureaucracy”.

key_points.verbatim: An AI arms race is a scenario in which two or more competitors—companies, policymakers in different countries, militaries—deploy increasingly powerful AI with inadequate oversight and control. The danger is that safer actors will be outcompeted by riskier ones.

key_points.verbatim: It also shows the importance of “anticipatory AI ethics”—identifying ethical issues as early as possible in the lifecycle of emerging technologies, developing norms and standards, and using those to actively shape the deployment of technologies and to minimize the likelihood of arms races.

key_points.verbatim: Unfortunately, the technical knowledge that is required to build capable AI models is already widespread, with many organizations sharing their complete code, data, and training methodologies.

factual_claims.claim: The diffusion of general-purpose technologies like electricity and computers takes decades to translate into measurable productivity gains.
AI models often fail in real-world deployment due to errors that are difficult to anticipate during testing, such as using future-dependent variables.
Human-in-the-loop control, where every decision requires human approval, often leads to human rubber-stamping or reduced automation benefits.
AI systems are currently deployed in high-stakes sectors without achieving perfect safety or alignment.
AI incident databases are currently sourced from news reports, which introduces selective and biased reporting of incidents.
The ESIGN Act of 2000 was instrumental in promoting digitization and e-commerce by establishing the legal validity of electronic signatures.
AI diffusion into safety-critical domains like healthcare is currently slow and relies on older statistical methods rather than modern deep learning.
Predictive models in high-stakes domains often fail due to 'data leakage' where future information is inadvertently included in training data.
Market success in the self-driving car industry has been strongly correlated with safety culture and outcomes.
AI models are inherently susceptible to adversarial vulnerabilities like prompt injection and jailbreaking that are difficult to fully eliminate.
The technical knowledge required to build capable AI models is already widespread and cannot be easily controlled through nonproliferation policies.
AI-driven scientific research can accelerate discoveries in fields like protein folding and drug discovery.
